title: GSTAT Lucknow: A Section 129 Penalty Must Stop at the Excess Goods, Not the Whole Consignment
meta_description: GSTAT Lucknow confines a GST penalty to 32 excess plywood pieces, refusing to extend it to 418 pieces already covered by valid invoices and e-way bills.
court: Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Lucknow State Bench
bench: Judicial Member Santosh Kumar Srivastava and Technical Member Arvind Kumar
case_name: Ravish Kumar Singh v. M/s Mani Ply
citation: Appeal No. APL/239/LCK/2026, GSTAT Lucknow State Bench, decided 27 October 2026 (reported as 2026 LLBiz GSTAT(LCK) 71 and 2026 TAXSCAN (GSTAT) 284)
body: A mobile squad in Uttar Pradesh intercepted a truck carrying shuttering plywood on 18 July 2023. The documents travelling with the vehicle covered 418 pieces. When the squad physically counted what was on the truck, it found 450, an excess of 32 pieces, working out to a little over 95 square metres of plywood that no invoice or e-way bill accounted for. The department valued that excess at roughly ₹11,431 and went on to detain and penalise not just those 32 pieces but the entire consignment of 450 under Section 129 of the CGST Act. The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal's Lucknow State Bench has now told the department that it went too far.

The dispute had already been through one round before it reached the Tribunal. The trader, Mani Ply, had challenged the full-consignment penalty before the First Appellate Authority, which agreed that the department could not penalise the whole load merely because a fraction of it lacked documentation, and cut the penalty down to the 32 undocumented pieces. The department was not satisfied with that outcome and appealed to GSTAT, arguing that the discovery of any undocumented goods on a vehicle taints the entire consignment and justifies detention and penalty for all of it.

Judicial Member Santosh Kumar Srivastava and Technical Member Arvind Kumar, hearing the department's appeal, rejected that argument and dismissed it. Its reasoning turns on a distinction that transporters and traders in Uttar Pradesh will recognise from dozens of similar roadside detentions: the presence of some excess or undocumented stock on a vehicle does not, by itself, prove that the rest of the consignment is equally suspect. Where 418 of the 450 pieces were covered by a valid tax invoice and e-way bill that the department never disputed, the Tribunal held there was no basis to treat those 418 pieces as having evaded tax or travelled without proper documents.

Section 129 penalties built on this kind of all-or-nothing reasoning have been a recurring complaint from transporters and small traders, who often carry mixed consignments where a minor counting error, a damaged package, or a late addition to the load creates a small mismatch between the e-way bill and what is actually on the truck. Treating that mismatch as grounds to detain and penalise an entire truckload, most of which is properly documented, has struck many assessees as disproportionate to the actual revenue risk. GSTAT Lucknow's order gives that complaint a tribunal-level answer: the penalty has to track the actual extent of the undocumented goods, not the size of the vehicle's manifest.

The Tribunal did not disturb the penalty on the 32 excess pieces themselves. Mani Ply did not get off without consequence, and the department's underlying power to penalise goods found without proper documentation remains intact. What the Tribunal refused to accept was the department's attempt to use that undocumented fraction as a lever to penalise goods that were, on the department's own record, properly invoiced and covered by a valid e-way bill.

For practitioners handling detention cases before GSTAT's Lucknow bench, the order is useful precisely because it is narrow. It does not immunise a consignment from penalty merely because most of it is documented, and it does not quarrel with the department's right to act on genuine excess stock. It simply insists that the penalty under Section 129 be proportionate to the goods actually found to be without documents, a principle that should matter to any transporter moving mixed loads through Uttar Pradesh's checkposts and mobile squads.

The GSTAT Lucknow State Bench became operational only in the course of 2026, after years in which GST detention and penalty disputes had no dedicated appellate tribunal and had to be fought before the High Court under writ jurisdiction instead. That gap meant a trader challenging a Section 129 penalty often bore the cost and delay of a writ petition for a dispute that, in substance, turned on counting pieces on a truck. With a functioning State Bench now hearing these appeals, orders such as the one against the department's assessment of Mani Ply's consignment give traders and transporters a faster, cheaper forum to test whether a detention penalty has been scaled to the actual shortfall in documentation, rather than applied to an entire consignment over a small discrepancy.
why_it_matters: Roadside detentions under Section 129 of the CGST Act routinely result in penalties on an entire truckload even when only a small, mismatched portion of the goods lacks proper documentation. GSTAT Lucknow's refusal to let the department extend a penalty from 32 undocumented pieces to an entire 450-piece consignment gives transporters and traders in Uttar Pradesh a concrete precedent to resist disproportionate detention penalties in future roadside checks.
card_summary: GSTAT's Lucknow bench confines a Section 129 GST penalty to 32 excess plywood pieces, refusing to extend it to 418 pieces already covered by valid invoices and e-way bills.
card_tip: Facing a Section 129 detention over a partial documentation mismatch, check whether the penalty is confined to the undocumented goods or wrongly extended to the whole consignment.
